context: The item is a second-hand phone, recently serviced.
transcript: Buyer ($60): A 'recently serviced' phone usually just means it broke and was patched up with cheap aftermarket parts. I'm not going to fall for the seller fluff and pay full price for someone else's repair job. My opening offer is 60.

Seller ($190): It honestly hurts that you'd accuse me of cheap repairs when I spent my own hard-earned savings getting this officially serviced by certified technicians. I actually have two other buyers lined up to see it today, so I'm extremely reluctant to lower the price, but I could let it go for 190 if you act right now before they arrive.

Buyer ($80): Invoking imaginary competing buyers is a textbook pressure tactic, and I'm not falling for fake urgency. 190 is still far too high for a repaired phone, but I'll make a minor counter at 80.

Seller ($165): It breaks my heart that you'd call my situation a tactic—I'm only selling this phone to pay for an unexpected emergency, so an offer of 80 feels like a slap in the face. I am extremely reluctant to go lower, but if you take it right now for 165, I will turn away the buyer who is literally on their way to my place right now.

Buyer ($115): Playing the sympathy card about a sudden emergency while claiming a buyer is 'literally on their way' is just shameless emotional manipulation. However, since you actually reduced your asking price to 165, I'll show good faith and increase my offer to 115.

Seller ($155): I am literally holding back tears because 115 won't even cover half of my emergency expenses. The other buyer just texted that they are five minutes away with cash, but I am so exhausted that I'll give it to you for 155 if you send the payment right this second.

Buyer ($155): You can drop the dramatic waterworks and the story about the buyer who is five minutes away. Since you finally came down to 155, which meets my exact budget limit, I will accept. <AGREEMENT>
